title: Navigation for a community sports club
metaTitle: Navigation a sports club member can use
excerpt: Club navigation should name the jobs a member is trying to finish, in their words. One path should reach membership or the schedule from every page.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table. A small group sharing one map, which is what club navigation has to be.
caption: Five people work on laptops around a wooden table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should club menu labels say?
faqs.answer: They should name errands: schedule, fees, sessions, coaches, visit. About, News, and More describe the website's furniture. If a beginner course has its own rules and its own crowd, Beginners can be a label of its own.

faqs.question: How many items belong in the header?
faqs.answer: Five to seven items is a menu a thumb can handle. Policies, minutes, and sponsor thanks can live in the footer. A primary path to membership or the schedule should stay visible, including on a phone, in the same words as the homepage.

faqs.question: Where should a gala or a one-off event go?
faqs.answer: Put it in a banner with a date. Leave the navigation stable so last year's members still recognize the doors. A top-level item that expires in a weekend trains people to distrust the menu.

sources.title: Influencing Title Links in Google Search

markdown:
Community sports club website navigation is a map of jobs a member is trying to finish. The labels should be words they already use, and one path should reach membership or the schedule from anywhere. Department names belong on a committee paper. They make a poor menu.

A new person arrives with an errand. Find Tuesday. Find the fee. Find the junior hour. The menu should read like those errands, in the club's plain speech.

## Jobs, named the way members say them

List the jobs before you list the pages you happen to have. See the schedule. Look at fees. Find a session I can join. Meet the coaches. Find the hall. Contact the right person. Each job that matters becomes a label. A job that rarely matters can live one level down, or inside the page it supports.

"About," "News," and "More" are leftovers from a template. They describe the website's furniture. They do not describe the errand. Replace them. Schedule. Fees. Sessions. Coaches. Visit. If the club has a beginner course with its own rules, "Beginners" can be a label of its own, because that is a job with a crowd.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) are organized so content is perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Navigation is an operable and understandable problem. People using a keyboard should reach every item. The words on the items should say where they go. A menu that only makes sense as icons, or as "click the crest," fails that standard and fails the hurried parent at the same time.

Keep the set short. Five to seven items is a menu a thumb can handle. If you need more, you have probably mixed jobs with archive. Season reviews, policies, and sponsor thanks can sit in a footer or on a single "club info" page linked once. They should not crowd out the schedule.

## One path to membership or the schedule

Choose the primary path and repeat it. A text link or button labeled in the same words as the homepage, present on every page, in the header. See the schedule. Membership. Whichever phrase the club says out loud. Consistency is the feature. A header that changes its verb on each template makes people relearn the club on every click.

The path should land on the fact, and it should do it in one tap. If "Membership" opens a page that explains the idea of belonging, and the fees are a further click, you have inserted a hallway. Hallways feel like a large site. They delay the decision. Let the label and the destination match. If the label says fees, the first screen of that page should show fees.

On a phone, the primary path must be visible without opening a drawer, if you can manage it. A sticky bar with Schedule and Fees is often enough. The full menu can live in a button labeled Menu, and that button should be a real button with a name, not a bare icon that a screen reader announces as "button." The guidelines' point about understandable controls applies to that icon as much as to the words beside it.

Do not hide the path inside "Join the family" if the thing they will see is a timetable. Say the timetable.

## Labels that survive a season

Write labels a new committee can keep. "Tuesday social" is better than a campaign name you will forget in October. If you run a short promotion, put it in a banner with an end date. Leave the navigation stable. People who joined last year still need the same doors, and a menu that changes its nouns every term trains them to distrust it.

Google's notes on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) warn against boilerplate titles that make pages indistinguishable, and against vague labels such as "Home" that fail to say what the page is. Navigation is the same promise, made in the chrome. Each destination should have its own clear name, and the menu label, the page heading, and the title should agree. "Fees" in the menu, "Fees for this season" on the page. A menu item called "Info" that opens a page titled "Welcome to our community" is three vague gestures in a row.

Test the labels on someone who does not sit on the committee. Read the menu aloud and ask where they would tap to bring a child on Thursday, and where they would tap to pay. If they hesitate, the label is still an internal joke. Fix the word. Do not add a tooltip.

## What lives one level down

Some items are real and secondary. Policies. A constitution. Meeting minutes. A shop for spare kit. These serve members who already decided, or a volunteer doing a job. Place them where they can be found on purpose, in the footer or a single Club page, with descriptive links. "Safeguarding policy" is a good link name. "Download" is not.

News belongs in navigation only if someone maintains it. A News item that opens on a post from two years ago suggests the club is closed. If the real news is the weekly schedule, the schedule is the news. Stop maintaining a second stream you cannot feed.

Sponsors can be a footer line. A top-level Sponsors item spends a primary slot on a page a prospective member did not come to read. Thank partners where the agreement says to thank them. Keep the map of jobs intact.

If the club runs two sports or two venues, the first label may need to split by sport or by place. "Hall" and "Outdoor" are jobs when both exist. A single Schedule that mixes them without headings will create wrong arrivals. The menu should admit the split the building already has.

## The phone menu is the real menu

Design the small screen first. Wide navigation that wraps into two elegant rows often collapses into a drawer that hides the one path you cared about. Open the drawer in the design and read the first six items. If Schedule is sixth, reorder. The drawer is still a list people scan from the top, and they scan it fast.

Tap targets need space. A row of text links crammed under a logo will be mis-tapped. Give each item a full row in the drawer. Show the current page. A person who is already on Fees should be able to see that, so they do not tap it again and assume the site is broken.

The header logo can return home. Home should then offer the same primary path within the first view. A logo that goes to a different mood, with a different button label, breaks the map at the moment of reorientation.

Reduced motion matters if you animate the drawer. A menu that swoops in and delays the tap is a small tax on every errand. A simple open and close respects people who have asked their device for less motion, and it respects people who are standing in a doorway trying to check a start time.

Two clubs that share a building need the menu to admit the split the building already has. Hall and field, or juniors and seniors, are jobs when a wrong tap produces a wrong arrival. Put the split in the label rather than in a paragraph the visitor has to open. A parent on a phone will not read a disclaimer under a single word like Sessions if that word hides two different doors.

Order the items by the first visit, then by the returning member. Schedule and fees lead. Coaches and the visit come next. Documents trail in the footer. Revisit that order at the start of the term, when a well-meaning volunteer will ask for a new top-level item called Gala. The gala can be a banner with a date. It should not rename the map for a weekend. Keyboard order should follow the visual order, so someone who tabs through the header meets Schedule before they meet a logo that goes nowhere useful.

Say the current page in the menu. A member who is already on the schedule should see that item marked, in text, so they do not tap it again and think the site ignored them. The mark can be as quiet as a heavier weight. It has to be more than color alone, so it survives for someone who does not see the color. That single cue makes the map feel trustworthy on the third visit, which is when a parent is checking a changed time.

## Navigation is a photograph's hallway

The menu also decides whether pictures can do their job. If Sessions is a real destination, that page can show people playing and how to start. If everything is buried under About, the photographs of play have nowhere honest to live, and the homepage becomes a dump of every picture the club owns. The next decision after the map is which pictures you are willing to publish, and which trophy shots you will refuse. That is [photography direction for a community sports club](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-community-sports-club).

A menu is part of the site you can ask a studio to shape with you. See [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) for the kind of web work that includes structure, not only a new coat of color. Bring the jobs your members already try to finish.
